name: Trilby

card.summary: A trilby is a short-brimmed felt hat that adds a classic, put-together silhouette to an outfit.
card.note: Style accessory; some forum posts also joke about weighted hats and height.

quick.overview:
A trilby is a narrow-brimmed hat, usually felt, with a brim angled down at the front and a crown slightly shorter than a fedora's. It is worn as a style accessory.

It appeals to people who want a vintage, dressed-up look; it can also frame the face and cover hair. Worn well, it is a quick way to change a whole outfit.
quick.how: People wear it with jackets, coats and smart-casual outfits, picking materials from rabbit-hair felt to tweed or straw. Some choose it to cover thinning hair or a bad hair day.
quick.risks: There is no health risk beyond fit and comfort. A forum post that joked of a trilby filled with gravel to add height was a tongue-in-cheek reply, not a documented method.

lead: The trilby is a short-brimmed hat traditionally made from rabbit-hair felt, now also from tweed, straw, cotton or wool. Lock & Co. describes its brim as shorter than a fedora's and angled down at the front [1].

The name comes from the stage adaptation of George du Maurier's 1894 novel Trilby, in which a hat of this style was worn in the first London production in 1895 [1][2]. In looksmaxxing and style circles it is discussed as an outfit accessory that gives a vintage, finished look, and one T Nation poster said he preferred a top hat or occasionally a trilby in the gym for the "classiest guy" effect, in jest [3].
No clinical research exists on trilbies and appearance.

paras: A trilby has a narrower brim than a fedora and a slightly shorter crown, and loosely resembles the Tyrolean hat [1].

The name derives from the 1895 London stage adaptation of Trilby, whose popularity led to the hat being called a trilby [1][2]. Wikipedia's account says it peaked in the late 1950s and early 1960s, receded around 1970, and was revived in later decades, though it flags parts of that history as needing sources [1]. Wearers it lists include Frank Sinatra and Peter Sellers as Inspector Clouseau [1].

Mentions are light. A 2009 T Nation thread about training hats had a poster joking about wearing a trilby at the gym [3]. A 2015 thread on increasing height included a reply that a heavy hat increased growth in some individuals by 2 percent and that researchers used a trilby filled with gravel; no source was given and no published study was located [4].
No studies found. The only scientific hits for the word are unrelated, such as a history article on mesmerism in fiction that discusses du Maurier's novel [5].

timeline.event: George du Maurier's novel Trilby is serialized [1][2].
A hat of this style is worn in the first London stage production and becomes known as a trilby [1].

lore.intro: Trilbies are mentioned occasionally on T Nation as a joke or minor style choice [3][4].

claims.claim: Wearing a weighted trilby adds height
claims.believers: A poster on T Nation wrote that a heavy hat increased growth in some individuals and that a trilby filled with gravel was used [4].
claims.experts: No published study was located testing hats and height; spinal compression and decompression over the day is a separate topic.
